subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Self-Driving, Eventually: What Autonomous Vehicles Teach About the Last Mile of Hard Tech
lesson.summary: Fully self-driving cars available everywhere to ordinary consumers were confidently promised on short timelines well before genuinely useful but still geographically and operationally limited deployments actually arrived, illustrating a hype pattern specific to technologies where the easy majority of a problem is solved quickly and the remaining portion turns out to be disproportionately hard.
lesson.body:
Automated driving systems made rapid, visible, genuinely impressive progress on highway driving, lane keeping, and controlled conditions, and that progress understandably generated confident public predictions that fully general, anywhere, any conditions autonomy was close behind. What actually followed was a much longer period of narrower, geographically limited deployments, specific cities, carefully mapped routes, favorable weather conditions, with the fully general version remaining elusive for far longer than the early, confident predictions suggested.

The specific mechanism behind this pattern is genuinely instructive and reaches well beyond cars: it is often called the last mile problem or the long tail problem. The bulk of ordinary driving situations gets handled well relatively early in a technology's development. The remaining edge cases, unusual weather, unpredictable pedestrian behavior, ambiguous construction zones, rare sensor failures, are each individually rare, but collectively common enough, and individually different enough from one another, that no single fix closes the gap, each one has to be handled essentially on its own terms. Progress on the easy majority of the problem creates the appearance of being nearly done, while the hard remaining fraction quietly turns out to represent the majority of the actual remaining engineering effort.

The connection to quantum computing is close in spirit to two ideas already covered in this course, the ten required breakthroughs and each breakthrough is uncertain. Early, dramatic quantum results, small scale demonstrations, narrow benchmark advantage claims chosen to favor the quantum system, are the equivalent of a self-driving demo handling a sunny, well mapped highway beautifully: real, impressive, and not yet evidence that the hard, unglamorous remaining engineering, error correction at scale, manufacturing consistency, integration into usable systems, will fall quickly just because the flashy part worked.

The lesson worth carrying forward is this: when a technology's demos keep getting more impressive but its actual deployment stays narrow, geofenced, benchmark only, lab scale, for far longer than early predictions implied, that persistence of narrowness is itself base rate evidence about how hard the remaining gap actually is, regardless of how good the demos look. Apply that same reading to quantum computing's own pattern of impressive but narrow demonstrations that have not yet generalized into broad, reliable, everyday usefulness.
